basis: Ushojo haliṣ turmeric matches haridrā with rhotic/dental cluster affrication and medial/final stress. It is the spice noun, independently distinct from the haridra yellow adjective13990; possible regional borrowing and suffix loss remain open.

Brokskat bude and Ushojo dwaš twelve preserve the two-plus-ten numeral family with differing contraction. Brokskat initial stress is explicit; Ushojo is now monosyllabic and unmarked, so it cannot test an old syllable position contrast.

Brokskat biẓaa and Ushojo bi twenty match viṁśatí with different retention/extension. Brokskat has final stress on aa, whereas Ushojo has a reduced unmarked monosyllable; the latter is also the base of productive vigesimal compounds.

Brokskat dave and Ushojo du two match the dva/dvau numeral paradigm. Brokskat's spelling may need a printed vowel reading; no accent is marked, and the old case/number form must not be selected based on its modern vowel alone.

Ushojo laalo very is identical to laalo many and shares that provisional bahura lexical-family analysis. Degree adverb use is a grammatical extension, not a second independent accent confirmation; strict exclusion remains until the initial l history is resolved.

Ushojo kooṭ village matches kōṭṭa fort/settlement through geminate simplification, with explicit long oo and no accent mark. It is a lexical replacement of dēśa/grāma in this semantic slot, not a different accent reflex of them.

Ushojo caṛege vomit (past) matches chardati with rd simplification and eg past formation. Aspiration differs in the field transcription; stress on the later stem/suffix belongs to the actual past form, so the link is root-family only.

Brokskat ẓaazis walk plausibly shares the yā/ya going root and recurring zis citation morphology, with palatalized onset. The exact verbal paradigm and separation from raazis say need primary confirmation; retain as provisional root-family evidence.

Brokskat ac̣hoo walnut matches akṣōṭa with kṣ affrication and loss of the final stop/syllable. The DB acute cannot specify mora in Brokskat and may come from an adjacent column; exact printed stress must be checked before quantitative coding.
Brokskat dus wash (transitive) matches dhuv washing root through contraction plus citation s. It is distinct from the passive dhūyate family; no accent is marked on this short citation.

Brokskat wɨɨ and Ushojo wi water match the udaká/wii water set through strong contraction, independently distinct from pānīya water. Brokskat marks length but no accent; Ushojo is short or lacks a length mark.

Brokskat bɨɨ we matches vayám/be contracted first-person plural forms, with explicit long vowel but no stress mark. Its separate merged ben village/we record needs splitting and source correction before counting.

Ushojo jola weaver is identical to its spider word and likely belongs to the jāla web/net occupational family, possibly through a regional julāhā-type loan. The human/animal polysemy is informative, but transmission and agent formation remain open; no direct inherited jā́la accent claim is made.

Ushojo aẓo wet matches ārdrá and is homophonous with its abhra-derived rain noun. Initial stress on the adjective is explicit; the two etyma must remain separate even though their modern strings and related meanings coincide.
Ushojo gum wheat matches gōdhū́ma after contraction of the two-root-vowel sequence and dh loss. No length or accent is marked; the token cannot test early versus late long-vowel accent.

Ushojo kare when is a temporal interrogative comparable with kárhi and Kundal karɛ, not kaláyati counts. Final stress is explicit and differs from the old barytone; any suffixal renewal or analogical interrogative pattern requires independent evidence.

Brokskat šoo and Ushojo šo white match śvētá with cluster reduction/contraction. The Brokskat acute is not automatically a mora reading; Ushojo is unmarked. Keep white separate from homophonous śubha good.

Ushojo koe and Brokskat koo who match the ká interrogative paradigm. Ushojo's unequal oe sequence with initial stress is not a simple long-vowel mora value; Brokskat koo has no written stress. Exact old case form remains grammatical, not lexical headword certainty.

Ushojo cai wife matches the straika/cei female set with str affrication and vowel contraction, rather than unextended strī alone. Initial stress in the ai sequence cannot be assigned early/late mora without source syllabification.

Brokskat šadzẓerii wife's brother matches the extended śvaśuriya/šaerī affinal kinship formation with final ii stress. The longer sibilant cluster may be a transcription issue;12767śvāśura is an alternative ultimate formation, so the exact suffix history remains open.

Ushojo jamaco wife's brother matches the jāmātṛ/jamc̣o affinal-kin set segmentally, but the kinship direction differs from son-in-law. It may be a reciprocal/extended affinal term; that semantic shift must be verified before using the final-stressed form as direct inherited accent evidence.

Ushojo paṣ wife's mother plausibly matches the p-initial śvaśrū/preṣ branch rather than ordinary ṣaṣ. The unusual initial consonant is independently paralleled by Palula preṣ but its phonological history remains open; no accent is marked.

Brokskat yuuno winter matches the Shina yon seasonal family grouped under ṛtuvanta. Initial stress and final o are explicit, but the ultimate compound reconstruction is not securely determined from this reduced form; hēmanta would require a different consonant history.

Brokskat koot wood matches kāṣṭha through ṣṭ simplification and rounded long vowel. Its apostrophe marks word stress only, and the exact final retroflex notation needs the printed cell; no independent mora contrast is claimed.

Ushojo paṣ wool matches pákṣman hair/wool through cluster reduction, independently distinct from its homophonous mother-in-law paṣ. No accent is marked; lexical homophony must not consolidate the two families.

Brokskat krom work matches kárman with metathesis and loss of the final syllable. The preserved cluster and short unmarked vowel are a useful control against treating all old clusters as sources of long-vowel tone.
Ushojo kaal year matches kālá time/year with explicit long aa and no accent mark. It is a different lexical source from varṣa and from regional Iranian sāl year.

Brokskat haldzuro yellow matches haridra yellow with an extended final o adjective formation and medial stress. The exact dz cluster and vowel reading need source verification; it must be separated from the haridrā turmeric noun13992.

Ushojo tu and Brokskat ti singular you match the tvam/tuvam second-person singular paradigm through contraction and vowel change. Neither is marked for accent; the modern case form is not necessarily the old nominative unchanged.

Brokskat tshur plural you plausibly belongs to the yuṣmad/tus plural paradigm, but the final r may be a source-reading issue and requires the printed cell. Retain the grammatical-family comparison provisionally; no accent is marked.
